title: One slit makes a fan. What do two slits 10 cm apart make? 7 bright bands, with dark water between.
description:
One slit makes a fan. What do two slits make? A ripple tank 80 x 58 cm seen from above: the same 2 cm ripples (wave speed 0.2 m/s at 10 Hz) roll up to the same wall. On top the wall has one slit 1 cm wide; below it has two slits 1 cm wide, 10 cm apart. A screen line 40 cm past the wall spans +-36 cm (+-42 degrees); the gold strip above it is the wave height squared, averaged over the last four periods, so the bright bands build up while you watch. 2D wave equation on a 1 mm grid (800 x 580 cells, 20 per wavelength), fourth-order Laplacian, leapfrog at Courant 1/3 (60 steps per period), a 4 cm absorbing sponge on every edge, a soft plane-wave source, a hard wall whose face absorbs like a beach except at the slits (so the incoming ripples travel instead of standing in front of it). Heights are shown on a square-root scale so the faint fans past the wall stay visible. Shown at 1/5 real speed. Deterministic, no seed.

Measured:
- two slits: 7 bright bands on the screen at 0, +-11.55, +-23.63 and +-36.73 degrees from the wall centre (0, +-8.17, +-17.50, +-29.85 cm); closed form d sin theta = n lambda gives 11.54, 23.58, 36.87 degrees (the outer band is pulled inward 0.14 degrees by the falling single-slit envelope)
- 6 dark bands between them at +-5.79, +-17.57 and +-30.12 degrees (+-4.05, +-12.67, +-23.21 cm); closed form d sin theta = (n + 1/2) lambda gives 5.74, 17.46, 30.00 degrees; the first dark band is 5.79 degrees off centre
- the dark bands hold at most 1.55% of the intensity of their neighbours; band heights 1.000, 0.952, 0.815, 0.611 of the centre
- one slit: 1 bright band with a flat top within 1% of the peak from -3.5 to +3.5 cm, falling to 0.922, 0.760, 0.593 and 0.528 of the peak at 10, 20, 30 and 35 cm on both sides, no dark band: the first dark direction of a 1 cm slit would need sin theta = lambda / a = 2
- two slits let through 1.990 times the summed intensity of one slit, and the centre of the screen is 3.804 times as bright (two waves in step: twice the amplitude, four times the intensity)
- incident wave amplitude 0.991 / 0.994 (one / two slits) in front of the wall with a standing-wave ratio of 1.020 / 1.028, so the beach sends back 1.0% / 1.4% of the amplitude
- the wave reaches the wall at 2.05 s of the video, the screen centre at 13.2 s and the screen ends at 15.9 to 16.7 s; the live counts settle at 1 bright, 0 dark from 13.67 s (one slit) and 7 bright, 6 dark from 16.18 s (two slits) to the end; at 30 s, 35 s and 40 s the ten-period averages give the same bands with angles within 0.01 degrees, and a twenty-period window changes nothing
- checks: at half the grid step (0.5 mm, 1600 x 1160 cells) the bands sit at +-11.54, +-23.59, +-36.71 (bright) and +-5.78, +-17.56, +-30.10 degrees (dark), within 0.04 degrees of the run shown; on screens 20 and 30 cm from the wall the same bands sit at 0.507 to 0.513 and 0.751 to 0.756 of their 40 cm positions (straight lines from the wall centre give 0.500 and 0.750), with 9 bright and 8 dark bands in the wider view (the 44.4 and 53 degree bands come into view); the one-slit profile has no minimum deeper than 0.55% of its peak on any screen

Why: each slit is narrower than the wavelength, so it sends out one smooth semicircular fan. With two slits, two fans of the same wave overlap. Along a direction where the path from one slit is longer than from the other by a whole wavelength, crest meets crest and the water swings high; half a wavelength longer, crest meets trough and the water stays flat. The bright directions satisfy d sin theta = n lambda, so with the slits 10 cm apart and the wavelength 2 cm the bands sit at sin theta = 0.2, 0.4, 0.6 and the dark ones at 0.1, 0.3, 0.5. One slit alone has no partner to cancel against, so its fan stays smooth.
